newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Jewish settlers take tourism ideas to Arafat.
newsitem.headline: Jewish settlers take tourism ideas to Arafat.

text.p: A group of Jewish settlers from the West Bank said on Wednesday they had met Palestinian President Yasser Arafat and he had given the green light for joint Israeli-Palestinian tourism projects.

"There are three, maybe four business opportunities on the table right now, and the Palestinians the settlers are in touch with were not willing to go ahead without Arafat's approval, and last night he gave the approval," said settler David Bedein.

A PLO official who attended the unusual 90-minute meeting in the Palestinian-ruled town of Bethlehem said that Arafat welcomed the settlers' support for coexistence and urged them to back establishment of a Palestinian state.

"Arafat told them that the most important thing was estabishing a state because coexistence with Palestinians under occupation has proved its failure," said the Palestinian official who declined to be identified.

Bedein said it was only logical for Israelis and Palestinians to work together on joint tourism ventures along a stretch from Bethlehem to Hebron he said was brimming with Jewish, Christian and Moslem holy sites.
He declined to elaborate on the ventures.

Bedein said 10 Israelis took part in the meeting, including Yehuda Waxman, father of Israeli soldier Nachshon Waxman who was kidnapped two years ago by Islamist militants and died in a gunfight between his Palestinian captors and Israeli soldiers.

"I believe that everyone there represented his own position. Everyone spoke a few moments and there were different stances. It was possible to speak openly, in a businesslike way and that's what people did," Waxman told Israeli army radio.
Most of the 130,000 Jews who live in settlements among the two million Palestinians of the West Bank and Gaza Strip oppose Israel's peace deals with Arafat which date back to 1993.

Palestinians view the settlements in the West Bank and Gaza illegal, and the United States, Israel's closest ally, called a defiant visit by right-wing Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu to a Jewish settlement on Tuesday a "very complicating factor".
